key_work: Habits of Mind: A Curriculum for Thinking (2000)
description: Costa and Kallick identify 16 cognitive dispositions — 'Habits of Mind' — that characterize intelligent, effective thinkers. Unlike skill-based frameworks, HOM focuses on the dispositions to know HOW to behave intelligently when encountering problems for which no easy answer exists. Each habit is a pattern of intellectual behaviors, not just a mental operation.
core_definition: A Habit of Mind is a disposition toward behaving intelligently when confronted with problems, the answers to which are not immediately known. A habit of mind involves knowing how to behave, when to use the strategy, and having the dispositions, motivations, and inclinations to deploy that behavior.
dewey_connection: Costa and Kallick explicitly situate HOM within Dewey's tradition of reflective thinking. Dewey argued that effective thinking is not reducible to skills but requires what he called 'attitudes' — dispositions to approach problems with curiosity, open-mindedness, and diligence. The 16 habits are a detailed elaboration of the dispositional dimension Dewey identified.
paul_elder_connection: Paul and Elder's 7 Intellectual Virtues and Costa/Kallick's 16 HOM overlap substantially. Both frameworks argue that CT requires not just skills but character. Key overlaps: Persisting ↔ Intellectual Perseverance; Managing Impulsivity ↔ Intellectual Humility; Thinking Flexibly ↔ Intellectual Open-mindedness; Thinking about Thinking ↔ Metacognition.

sixteen_habits.core_description: Sticking to a task when the solution is not immediate. Not giving up. Employing systematic methods of problem analysis and solution.
behavioral_indicators: Continues working when confused or uncertain
Tries different approaches when the first fails
Sets incremental goals to maintain progress
Uses internal dialogue to maintain motivation
absence_indicators: Says 'I can't do this' and stops
sixteen_habits.dewey_phase: All phases — persisting is what sustains inquiry

sixteen_habits.core_description: Thinking before acting. Deliberately resisting the urge to respond immediately. Forming a plan before beginning.
behavioral_indicators: Pauses before answering difficult questions
Counts to ten before reacting in charged situations
Thinks through multiple approaches before beginning
Asks clarifying questions before starting
sixteen_habits.dewey_phase: Phase 1/2 — before moving from felt difficulty to intellectualization
sixteen_habits.system_connection: Managing impulsivity = engaging System 2 over System 1 default

sixteen_habits.core_description: Understanding others' points of view. Holding one's own thoughts in abeyance while genuinely attending to another's thinking. Paraphrasing others' ideas before responding.
behavioral_indicators: Paraphrases before responding
Asks questions to understand rather than to rebut
Attends to emotional content as well as propositional content
Holds own views tentatively while listening
absence_indicators: Formulates rebuttal while the other is still speaking
Responds to what they expected to hear rather than what was said

sixteen_habits.core_description: The capacity to change perspectives, consider alternatives, generate multiple approaches to a problem, and hold multiple viewpoints simultaneously.
behavioral_indicators: Generates multiple alternatives before committing
Takes opposing perspectives seriously
Changes approach when initial strategy isn't working
Uses lateral thinking and analogical reasoning
absence_indicators: Treats one's own perspective as the only valid one

sixteen_habits.core_description: Awareness of one's own thinking processes. Ability to plan, monitor, and evaluate one's own cognitive strategies. Knowing what one knows and doesn't know.
behavioral_indicators: Can articulate own thinking strategies
Monitors comprehension while reading or listening
Knows when understanding has broken down
Reflects on cognitive performance after completing tasks
absence_indicators: Cannot describe how they solved a problem
Unaware of errors in own thinking
sixteen_habits.dewey_connection: Metacognition is Dewey's reflective consciousness applied to one's own reasoning
sixteen_habits.paul_elder_trait: All Intellectual Standards — applied to one's own thinking

sixteen_habits.core_description: The drive to produce excellence — checking work, reviewing, revising, refusing to accept less than quality performance from oneself.
behavioral_indicators: Reviews work before submitting
Sets personal standards that exceed minimum requirements
Corrects own errors voluntarily
Asks 'is this my best work?'

sixteen_habits.core_description: Finding out what is unknown. Asking questions for information, clarity, challenge, and exploration. Generating genuine intellectual problems, not just reciting known answers.
behavioral_indicators: Generates original questions, not just answers
Asks 'what if?' and 'I wonder why?'
Formulates testable hypotheses
Seeks to understand rather than to complete assignments
absence_indicators: Asks only convergent questions with known answers
sixteen_habits.dewey_phase: Phase 1/2 — the generative beginning of inquiry

sixteen_habits.habit: Applying Past Knowledge to New Situations
sixteen_habits.core_description: Using prior experience, knowledge, and learning to address novel situations. Transfer — the ultimate goal of education.
behavioral_indicators: Draws analogies from prior experience
Recognizes patterns across contexts
Asks 'what do I know that's like this?'
Adapts previously successful strategies to new contexts
absence_indicators: Treats each problem as completely novel
Cannot connect current to prior learning
Requires all explicit instruction for each new context
sixteen_habits.dewey_phase: Phase 3 — hypothesis formation draws on prior experience

sixteen_habits.habit: Thinking and Communicating with Clarity and Precision
sixteen_habits.core_description: Using careful, precise language. Avoiding vagueness, over-generalizations, and ambiguous communication. Defining terms, supporting claims with evidence.
behavioral_indicators: Avoids vague quantifiers ('many', 'some', 'they')
Defines key terms explicitly
Qualifies claims appropriately
Speaks in specific, concrete terms rather than abstractions

sixteen_habits.core_description: Using the full sensory apparatus — paying attention to texture, sound, smell, spatial relationships — in observation and inquiry. Cultivating perceptual acuity.
behavioral_indicators: Uses multiple observational modes
Notices nuances others miss
Uses data sources beyond language (visual, auditory, kinesthetic)
Observes carefully before interpreting
sixteen_habits.dewey_phase: Phase 3 — observation as the basis for hypothesis

sixteen_habits.core_description: Generating novel ideas, approaches, and solutions. Not being satisfied with the conventional. Trying different ways.
behavioral_indicators: Generates multiple unconventional alternatives
Approaches familiar tasks in new ways
Asks 'what if we tried...?'
Finds creative solutions when standard methods fail
sixteen_habits.lipman_connection: Creative thinking — one of Lipman's three thinking modes

sixteen_habits.core_description: Finding what is beautiful, mysterious, and awesome in the world. Maintaining intellectual curiosity. Approaching problems with intrinsic motivation and genuine interest.
behavioral_indicators: Expresses genuine delight in discovery
Explores voluntarily beyond required inquiry
Maintains curiosity about phenomena beyond immediate problem
Connects intellectual work to larger fascinations
absence_indicators: Asks only 'will this be on the test?'

sixteen_habits.core_description: Living on the learning edge of one's comfort zone. Accepting challenges without knowing if success is guaranteed. The willingness to be wrong.
behavioral_indicators: Ventures opinions when uncertain
Attempts novel approaches
Accepts failure as information rather than catastrophe
Takes intellectual positions that may be challenged
absence_indicators: Only answers when certain of success

sixteen_habits.core_description: Laughing at one's own mistakes and the incongruities of the world. Using humor to reduce defensive barriers to learning. Finding the comic in the cosmic.
behavioral_indicators: Laughs at own errors without defensiveness
Uses humor constructively in group work
Recognizes absurdity and incongruity
Takes ideas seriously but not self too seriously
absence_indicators: Cannot recover gracefully from being wrong

sixteen_habits.core_description: Being able to work collaboratively and contribute to group thinking. Learning from others. Combining intellectual efforts.
behavioral_indicators: Contributes to and builds on others' ideas
Shares reasoning processes, not just answers
Seeks input from others on own thinking
Creates intellectual community rather than competition
absence_indicators: Does not seek or give feedback on thinking
Views intellectual work as purely individual
sixteen_habits.lipman_connection: Community of Inquiry — one of Lipman's core constructs

sixteen_habits.core_description: Having a growth mindset toward one's own intelligence and capacities. Recognizing that one is never fully formed. Approaching each new situation with curiosity.
behavioral_indicators: Updates beliefs when warranted by evidence
Treats criticism as resource
Explores areas of ignorance without shame
Maintains a beginner's mind
absence_indicators: Fixed mindset — believes intelligence is static

app_usage.exercise_feature: Each habit generates a distinct reflection exercise type
app_usage.self_assessment: 16 habits as a self-assessment checklist — 'which habits am I strong in? which need development?'
app_usage.portfolio_feature: Track growth in individual habits across multiple exercises
app_usage.template_feature: HOM as a metacognitive reflection template after any learning activity
